entries.title: Jensen Huang’s Return Shows Nvidia Is Too Big to Police
entries.summary: Nvidia’s place at the center of the US economy may have outweighed concerns about its CEO’s ties to a suspected Chinese intelligence asset, national security and foreign policy experts say.
entries.content:
Nvidia’s decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO signals that the chipmaker may have grown too important to the stock market for the US government to hold it accountable for national security lapses, intelligence and export-control experts warn WIRED. The move also undercuts the warnings Washington routinely issues to American companies and foreign governments about Beijing’s pursuit of US technology, they say.

Nvidia’s board brought back Huang on Monday, 11 days after he resigned amid revelations of extramarital affairs—one of them with Alice Huang, a woman US intelligence suspects has ties to China’s Ministry of State Security. The board said input from “senior levels of the United States government” left it confident that his return poses no national security risk.

President Donald Trump told The Wall Street Journal he lobbied the board directly and through intermediaries, and that Nvidia’s falling share price helped his case. The board acted before its own investigation of Huang had concluded, and while the Justice Department is pursuing a criminal probe of Megaspeed—a Singapore company Alice Huang once ran—over the alleged diversion of Nvidia chips to China. Alice Huang is also under investigation, according to director of national intelligence Jay Clayton.

The experts tell WIRED they worry more about the precedent Huang’s return sets than about Huang himself. Some say the scrutiny now on him makes further compromise unlikely. But Beijing may already have gained insight into Nvidia’s chip designs and its private conversations with the White House and Congress, or, through Megaspeed, obtained the chips themselves, they say, and no one has publicly established what, if anything, it got.

Several want to know who gave the board its assurances and on what basis, and whether the government ran a counterintelligence damage assessment or simply made a political judgment. They also say the administration has repeatedly failed to enforce its own export controls, and that when intelligence concerns appear to yield to market pressure, US warnings about China start to sound negotiable, to Beijing’s benefit.

“If intelligence assessments are seen to be overridden, selectively interpreted, or publicly dismissed for political or commercial reasons, this could undermine long-term confidence in the independence of national security institutions,” says Tahlia Peterson, a cyber and technology research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a London defense think tank. “That would be damaging to US national security, and potentially advantageous to Beijing.”

Advisers briefed Trump at least twice on Alice Huang’s links to Chinese intelligence before the affair became public, and both times he played down their concerns, The New York Times reported Sunday. When the Journal asked him on Monday about Republican lawmakers who say Huang’s return endangers national security, Trump pointed to Nvidia’s rebounding stock.

“Some tech companies have become so big—and so important to the stock market—that Washington is reluctant to hold them accountable for national security lapses,” says Edward Fishman, director of the Council on Foreign Relations’ Maurice R. Greenberg Center for Geoeconomics.

Fishman sees a parallel in Wall Street’s slow reckoning with sanctions. “It took years of aggressive enforcement to get banks to take US sanctions compliance seriously,” he says. “We haven’t seen anything comparable in the tech sector, which helps explain why US export controls remain so weak and leaky.” Reinstating Huang on the administration's assurances before Nvidia’s own investigation has concluded “does not inspire confidence that meaningful enforcement is coming,” he says.

Emily Kilcrease, a former deputy assistant US trade representative who now directs the Energy, Economics, and Security program at the Center for a New American Security, says the administration’s record gives little reason to take those assurances at face value. “We cannot rely on the administration’s judgment, as it has repeatedly failed to enforce export controls over the past year,” she says.

On Monday, the Commerce Department added Megaspeed to its trade blacklist, and the administration has recently moved to tighten rules on China’s AI industry. But Kilcrease says it acted only under pressure. “Given the poor track record on export controls and their broader accommodationist stance toward China, it’s fair to ask whether they are willing to really enforce the new controls,” she says.

The board’s assurances appear to have come mostly from the Justice Department. Attorney general Todd Blanche allegedly told Trump and vice president JD Vance on Saturday that Huang was neither a target nor a subject of any department investigation, and that the department had no evidence he had broken the law or posed a national security risk, the Journal reports. Vance then reportedly sought assurances for the board that the administration did not consider Huang a threat and that he would not face criminal charges. Trump told the Times he also consulted Clayton before pushing for Huang’s return. (“I can’t do this and then all of a sudden have somebody get indicted,” he said.)

Nvidia did not immediately respond to WIRED’s request for comment.

Whether Huang broke any laws is a separate question from whether Beijing gained anything through him. “Did [the assurances] reflect a counterintelligence damage assessment by the intelligence community or the FBI, or were they political in nature?” says Jessica Brandt, a senior fellow for technology and national security at the Council on Foreign Relations who previously directed the Foreign Malign Influence Center at the Office of the Director of National Intelligence. “Lawmakers should press on that.”

Senior officials may have seen intelligence that isn’t public, so the assurances shouldn’t just be dismissed, says Sunny Cheung, a China studies fellow at the Jamestown Foundation. “However, we still don’t know who provided those assurances, what evidence they reviewed, or how they reached their conclusion, particularly when Nvidia’s own independent investigation remains unfinished,” he says.

Lawmakers appear to have seen little of that evidence. At a briefing this month by CIA director John Ratcliffe and Clayton that was scheduled to cover Iran, lawmakers pressed for answers about Huang, and the responses left some of them puzzled, according to the Times. A follow-up briefing for senior national security staff was postponed.

Cheung says the Ministry of State Security may not have needed Nvidia’s secrets to profit from the relationship. “From a counterintelligence perspective, I think people are too focused on whether Jensen handed over trade secrets,” he says. “China’s Ministry of State Security wouldn’t necessarily need Nvidia’s next-generation chip blueprints to benefit from access to him.” Insight into Huang’s direct conversations with the president, senior officials, and other top tech executives, along with his views on China and Taiwan and his role in Washington’s export-control debate, “could already be extremely valuable to Beijing,” he says.

Brandt sees the same mix of risks. “Information about Nvidia’s proprietary chip designs could help China advance its own chip design efforts,” she says. “Insight into Nvidia’s conversations with the White House and Congress could help Beijing anticipate where US export control policy is headed.” Investigators should also ask whether Alice Huang compromised Huang’s devices, what security clearance he held, and whether he still holds it, she says.

Huang successfully lobbied the Trump administration to roll back restrictions on Nvidia’s chip sales to China and negotiated a deal giving the US government a 25 percent cut of sales of certain chips approved for export there, the Times has reported. In April, minister of state security Chen Yixin made overcoming the “blockades” that limit China’s access to key technologies like AI a sixth core mission for his ministry, known as the MSS. Alice Huang’s network of chip-buying companies “lines up precisely” with that mission, Matt Pottinger, who served as deputy national security adviser during Trump’s first term, told the paper.

“A further question is whether Alice Huang was tasked by Chinese intelligence to influence Jensen Huang's views or approach to US export restrictions on China, and, if so, to what extent she succeeded,” Peterson says. The Journal also reported that the intelligence is inconclusive on whether she was actively tasked to collect information on Huang, and Cheung says “whether any such information was obtained or influence exercised remains unproven.”

Megaspeed’s purchases are better documented. A Malaysian subsidiary bought at least $4.8 billion worth of equipment containing Nvidia chips between June 2024 and February 2026, according to trade records the Times reviewed. Its subsidiaries have also served Chinese clients, including Alibaba. US intelligence indicates that Alice Huang was in contact with an MSS officer from spring 2025 until this fall, and that her business partner, Kang Wei, also worked with the agency, the paper reported Sunday. Her network has been linked to efforts to supply Nvidia chips to China’s state-owned military contractors. Enough has been reported to suggest that Huang, “wittingly or not, may have played a role in helping Megaspeed as it sought access to advanced Nvidia chips,” Kilcrease says.

Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Nicholas Eftimiades, a former CIA and Defense Intelligence Agency officer who teaches homeland security at Penn State Harrisburg, says Huang himself poses no security risk. Now that the relationship is public, he says, Huang has little chance of unwittingly passing along more information about US government policy or Nvidia’s board deliberations. Peterson agrees that scrutiny from Nvidia’s board, its compliance staff, federal agencies, and Congress likely limits any further exposure. But “we are still in the dark as to whether any sensitive information may already have been compromised,” she says, “or whether any resulting harm can be identified or mitigated.”

Huang’s defenders have repeatedly noted that he never received a defensive briefing, a warning the government sometimes gives Americans whom foreign intelligence services target. Nvidia’s board says its investigation will continue with Huang’s cooperation, and the company is searching for a chief compliance officer. A committee of independent directors is examining whether Huang shared corporate or national security information with Alice Huang. The board has also formed a new committee of independent directors to oversee trade compliance and national security risks.

Peterson says the company’s leadership matters. “Nvidia is an exceptionally important company, and there are legitimate arguments about the implications of losing its leadership at a critical moment in the global AI race,” she says. “But those considerations should not determine the conclusions of national security investigations.”

Trump told CNBC Monday that keeping the United States ahead of China made reinstating Huang imperative. “If we didn't do this, I could see China coming in and saying to Jensen, ‘Hey, how would you like to come to China?’” he said.

For Brandt, the bigger cost may come with Washington’s next warning. “This erodes the credibility of US government warnings about China’s technological ambitions and how far it will go to achieve them,” she says. “How will those warnings land going forward, both with our own companies and with foreign governments? We risk making a hard problem harder: emboldening Beijing while weakening our own defenses.”

That cost extends to the allies Washington depends on to police its controls, adds Sarah Bauerle Danzman, an associate professor of international studies at Indiana University’s Hamilton Lugar School. The Commerce Department has few enforcement agents abroad to monitor transshipment, she says, so the system relies on partner countries to run checks and share information about problematic buyers. Singapore says it repeatedly raised concerns with US authorities in this case.

“These types of incidents make such cooperation more difficult to sustain,” Bauerle Danzman says.

Huang and Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter have agreed to closed-door, transcribed interviews with three House committees on December 1 and 2. “The legal and reputational risk of hiring a CEO who may very well be convicted in the United States or other nations of violating espionage and export control laws is now [borne] by the board of Nvidia, but the national security risk is passed along to the United States military and its citizens,” Senator Kevin Cramer, a North Dakota Republican, said on X.

“I think Congress has gotten fed up,” says Kilcrease, who cites bipartisan concern about Megaspeed and what she calls the administration’s broader accommodation of China. “We can expect hearings and investigations from multiple committees, and Congress is highly motivated to pass legislation to tighten export controls, increase its oversight of administration decisions, and bolster enforcement.”

“Jensen may be back, and he should not be presumed guilty of wrongdoing,” Cheung says. “But his reinstatement should not be mistaken for a clean bill of health. Nvidia and the administration still have important questions to answer.”

entries.title: 16 Best Black Friday Headphone Deals (2026): Up to 57% Off
entries.summary: Get up to 57 percent off some of my favorite headphones and earbuds from Apple, Sony, Nothing, and more.
entries.content:
It is a great time to buy a new pair of headphones. Brands have largely finished launching their latest models for the year, and I'm seeing some stellar Black Friday deals on new and older headphones alike. I've been reviewing headphones (and covering deals) for more than four years, so I have a good handle on what's worth opening your wallet for. (Spoilers: it's Sony and Bose this year).

All the deals below are WIRED-tested products we stand by, including wireless earbuds and over-ear headphones. For more Black Friday deals, check out our guides to the Best Black Friday TV Deals and the Best Black Friday Mattress Deals.

Updated November 24: I added new products on sale from Bose, Samsung, Sony, and Soundcore. I also updated pricing on other deals.

Best Earbud Deals

Apple AirPods Pro 3 are the best wireless earbuds not only for anyone with an iPhone—but also for anyone who wants to keep things simple. They sound great and have some of the best active-noise-canceling (ANC) and transparency modes on the market. They also seamlessly sync with all of your Apple devices. At $100 off, it's the lowest price they've ever been at.

This is the lowest price I’ve ever seen on one of my favorite pairs of wireless earbuds. The Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro have one magic trick: call quality. To put it simply, I sound better talking on calls using these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, and it’s not a close competition. Beyond that, they’re solid all-rounders, with good noise-canceling, sound quality, and versatility.

Want workout earbuds that won't fall out? Get these Beats Powerbeats Pro 2. They're some of the more secure-fitting earbuds I've ever tested. Plus, they have great noise-canceling, transparency, and even built-in heart-rate sensors, so you can track your workout even if you left your fitness tracker at home.

The Nothing Ear (3a) are one of our favorite pairs of earbuds under $100, and 30 percent off is the biggest discount I've ever seen for them so far. They have a semi-transparent design and bold colors that stand out from the crowd (particularly the yellow version). While the automated noise-canceling isn't the best, it's hard to fault them at this new low price.

  • Samsung Galaxy Buds 4 Pro for $180 ($70 off): Our go-to earbuds of choice for anyone with a Samsung Galaxy phone.
  • Shokz OpenFit 2+ for $100 ($100 off): Great open ear headphones at an exceptional discount.
  • Sony WF-1000XM6 for $248 ($82 off): If you want excellent sound quality in your ANC earbuds, these Sony earbuds have dynamic bass and clear, detailed treble.

Best Over-Ear Headphone Deals

My main gripe with the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen) is price. At 45 percent off (their lowest price ever), that complaint vanishes, making this a top headphone deal to shop. The headphones are exceedingly comfortable and have stellar ANC—far better than basically every other set of headphones at this new low price of $200.

Did you hear the news? Sony made a version two of their cult-classic Sony WH-1000XM4 headphones. This is the first time they are on sale, and at $200, are one of the best deals this Black Friday. They have stellar sound, great noise-canceling, a comfortable fit, and a convenient, folding design well-suited for travel.

The Nothing Headphone (1) are a home run in looks and sound, and they are at their lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday. They’re solid noise cancelers with a bold, transparent design on the ear cups that's somehow techy, retro, and futuristic-looking. Among their best features are the on-ear controls, namely the clicky wheel that adjusts volume and the flat rocker paddle that you can push back and forth to move to the previous track or skip ahead, respectively.

The budget Nothing Headphone (a) and premium Nothing Headphone (1) Pro are also on sale, but the Headphone (1) is the most appealing deal in my view.

AirPods Max 2 are excellent over-ear headphones for Apple fans, but the $550 sticker price is frankly absurd. Thankfully, they are almost always a little bit on sale, including now. This is far from the best deal I've seen on these headphones, and I do expect the price to dip further during Black Friday sales events, so I would add them to my cart and wait to pull the trigger.

My top over-ear headphone pick, the best-in-class Sony WH-1000XM6, is at its lowest price ever this Black Friday. These headphones are amazing across the board, with their high comfort, superior sound quality, and great noise-canceling capability.

  • Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd Gen) for $369 ($80 off): These are the best ANC headphones you can buy (read our review here), but the discount could be better.
  • CMF Headphone Pro for $49 ($30 off): CMF is Nothing's sub-brand, and this is a great deal on surprisingly capable, budget headphones.

entries.title: 11 Things Jensen Huang Actually Said at His First All-Hands Back at Nvidia
entries.summary: The newly reinstated CEO discussed his daily therapy sessions, his reputation as a “tech bro,” his disdain for succession planning, and his relationship with President Trump.
entries.content:
Jensen Huang is going to therapy for 90 minutes a day and rethinking his management style, and he says that violating Nvidia’s code of conduct isn’t necessarily a fireable offense. That’s just some of what the newly returned Nvidia CEO told staff during his first all-hands meeting on Tuesday.

Here are some of the most striking things Huang said during the meeting, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

On self-improvement: “I go to therapy every day for an hour and a half. And it’s been helping me a lot.”

On accountability: “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back. Apparently, I’m a tech bro, and because I wear a super nice jacket, that I’m above the law, and I’m above the code of conduct. That is not true. It won’t be tolerated, and it wasn’t tolerated here.”

“If one of you were to violate a code of conduct, what does that mean? If you were ever to violate a code of conduct, it is not appropriate. I just wanted you to know, it is not right, it's not appropriate, it won’t be tolerated. But ‘it won’t be tolerated’ does not mean the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door. Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments. And your management team will still make the decision. That is what is in the best interest of the company and its employees, with all the facts and circumstances.”

On his management style: “The intensity I bring elevates everybody else. But I can go too far. When I go too far, it hurts people, it belittles them, it disempowers them. And that’s not right. And so I need to go figure out how I’m going to bring the intensity, the crazy intensity, to the field.”

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact WIRED reporters securely on Signal at ChaoticGoode.12 & Peard33.24

On women at Nvidia: “I believe we need to create and continue to sustain a safe environment for all of our women. And if I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it. We will not tolerate that.”

On succession: “All day long, this company can run autonomously, and you saw it. I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute, and deliver on financial results.”

“I also didn’t believe in succession planning. Let that sink in. I don’t believe in succession planning. I think it’s flawed. The idea of succession planning is not flawed. What people think succession planning means is flawed.”

“There’s a reason why we don’t have succession planning; it’s not because we are unaware of the word. I’m the longest-running tech CEO in history.”

On politics: “There [were] also rumors that apparently I’m back because the highest levels of our government wanted me back. That is also completely untrue. Our board of directors performed their duty as they should have.”

“It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang told employees. “He gloats about Nvidia. You know he does. But there’s a question about politics. Are we now political? Are we partisan? I wanna be very clear with you. President Trump is the United States president. He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president be informed about how he could make decisions that are in the best interest of our country … We have to do it, and whoever the next president is will be my president, and I will do exactly the same.”

“Don’t think for a second that politics ever plays a role in this company, not even a little bit. We are the most apolitical company. I don’t love that we talk about politics here. Take it home. I love that we talk about work here.”

entries.title: iRestore Elite Laser Hair Growth System Review: Husband-Approved
entries.summary: Here’s how his scalp fared after several months of using the iRestore Elite Laser Hair Growth System.
entries.content:
Easy daily use. Lots of LEDs and medical-grade lasers. Simple to wear. FDA-cleared tech. Results started to appear within a month.

TIRED

Must be used consistently. Portable battery is an extra $99.

The Aging Process is hard. It’s jarring, for example, when the luscious, flowing locks of your youth start to disappear before your very eyes. But there's nothing to do about this natural hair loss—or is there? While still the subject of ongoing research, red-light therapy has been used to treat inflammation, pain relief, and wrinkles, and—as it turns out—it may also help with hair regrowth. It’s also a much more accessible option than flying to Istanbul for a full-on hair transplant.

I learned about iRestore’s Elite Laser Growth Hair System after it came across my TikTok FYP. My algorithm likely served it to me because of my own hair woes (scalp irritation and eczema). Upon learning more about the system, I hoped it could help me with cell regeneration and kill off the bacteria causing flares on my scalp.

However, an even better test subject stood before me: my sweet husband, who is dealing with a rapidly receding hairline. So I roped him into testing this laser helmet—for science, of course. And to better understand said science, I spoke with Zakia Rahman, MD, FAAD, a clinical professor of dermatology at Stanford University School of Medicine.

The Scientific Crown

Photograph: Julia Forbes

Red-light therapy didn’t start as a treatment for antiaging and recovery. It actually came about as an accidental solution for hair loss in the 1960s, when Hungarian scientist Endre Mester was researching whether exposure to red light could treat cancer in hairless mice. Imagine his surprise when the mice started growing hair.

Red-light therapy has come a long way since then. According to Rahman, red-light wavelengths are thought to activate the mitochondria in skin cells, which may encourage an uptick in the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP) to promote new growth. Red-light therapy may also improve blood flow to hair follicles.

Photograph: Julia Forbes

Importantly, iRestore's devices are FDA-cleared—a safety designation from the US Food and Drug Administration indicating that a product is “substantially equivalent” to another legally marketed device. There are three hair-growth devices in iRestore's lineup: the entry-level Essential ($425), the mid-tier Professional ($799), and the Elite ($1,699). Each contains iRestore’s proprietary Lumitech technology, which combines LED lights and medical-grade lasers. These laser diodes, called Vixo lasers, operate in the range of 655 to 680 nanometers (nm). (Preliminary studies with mice have shown that using red light in the 600- to 660-nm range, and infrared wavelengths in the 800- to 850-nm range, can promote cell regeneration, pain relief, and more.)

The idea is that this dynamic duo of lights and lasers can penetrate deeper into the skin than ordinary red light with lasers, while the LEDs ensure light is distributed across the scalp for maximum efficacy. Together, they reach a maximum of 2,500 milliwatts (mW) in the Elite, compared to the Professional's 1,410 mW and Essential's 600 mW.

Photograph: Julia Forbes

The Elite is iRestore’s top-of-the-line offering and has the most LEDs of the three laser hair-growth systems, with 500 diodes in total—that's 300 lasers and 200 LEDs. The Essential has 51 lasers and 69 LEDs for a total of 120 diodes, while the iRestore Professional has 82 lasers and 200 LEDs for a total of 282 diodes. The Elite was also designed to cover more of the scalp than the other two models and requires 12 minutes of daily use, while the Professional and Essential require 25 minutes every other day.

If price is not a factor, the Elite is the no-brainer choice due to its higher-concentrated light therapy, shorter use time, and potentially faster results.

Growth Spurt

Photograph: Julia Forbes

The helmet arrived in hefty red packaging containing the helmet, a portable battery pack (annoyingly, this is a $99 add-on purchase), a charging cord, and a red-and-black zippered travel case. It feels very fragile, and I wouldn't throw it around—then again, you probably wouldn't plan to shove such an expensive device in the back of your bathroom vanity.

During the daily 12-minute sessions with the Elite helmet, you'll feel as if you're sitting under bright, hot sunlight. The remote displays a countdown of how many minutes you have left, and it beeps once the cycle is complete. Because I was testing the helmet to treat my dry scalp and eczema, I grew increasingly concerned with every passing minute of feeling warmer and warmer. (Sweating is a big no-no for eczema, so I wasn’t thrilled to experience this side effect.) With time, my husband was able to get used to the heat-lamp effect, as it’s not painful, just initially uncomfortable.

Photograph: Julia Forbes

Within the first two weeks of continuously using the helmet, I was thrilled to see baby hairs begin to pop up around my husband's hairline. The growth continued through two months of regular use. The top of his crown had more volume and overall hair density, while new growth appeared in the more drastically affected areas near his forehead. While the additional hair didn’t completely cover his scalp, the change was stark enough for old college friends and family members to remark on how good his hair looked.

The effects aren't permanent, though. Unfortunately, my husband stopped his iRestore routine after a few months due to travel. While the iRestore Elite comes with a case that makes it super portable, my husband was nervous about misplacing it while we were on the go. (Also, the thing takes up a decent amount of space.) Unfortunately, stopping the treatments reversed the progress in a matter of weeks. Just like that, he was back to square one.

Rahman likens this phenomenon to the importance of a commitment to a healthy daily diet and regular exercise; one instance of either won't make a difference in your health. Rather, consistency is required to drive results. When I told her that my husband's hair growth had fallen off, she strongly encouraged us to pick it back up.

A Hairy Situation

In addition to using the red-light therapy helmet as recommended, iRestore suggests adding thickening haircare products (shampoo, conditioner, supplements, and serum) to your regimen to get the best results. The star ingredient in the serum and shampoo is plant-based Redensyl, which is meant to fortify hair follicles during their regrowth. Additional elements—like the shampoo's castor oil and biotin, and the conditioner's vegan keratin and argan oil—act as natural strengtheners.

The supplements contain natural dihydrotestosterone (DHT) blockers derived from saw palmetto. These blockers work to prevent the enzyme (5-alpha reductase) from transforming testosterone into DHT. In essence, this hormone is a driver of pattern hair loss and can lead to general inactivity in hair growth.

Photograph: Julia Forbes

The supplements, strengthening serum, shampoo, and conditioner come included with the purchase of the iRestore Elite. The extras didn't seem to boost my results but may have supported my husband's regular use of the helmet. (Full disclosure: He was also using his usual Rogaine throughout this entire process.)

Ultimately, these included products are a nice bonus, but you don't need to go out of your way to buy them from iRestore or to replenish your stash. Plenty of anti-hair-loss treatments are available, including oral and topical medications and hair-transplant procedures. All have their merits in slowing hair thinning and promoting fuller hair. Even so, “combination therapy will work better than a stand-alone," says Rahman, in response to my question about whether red-light therapy could work as an isolated treatment or if it's best to include it as part of a multicomponent regimen. Essentially, the potential benefits of red-light therapy only stand to increase when you supplement it with minoxidil and other highly researched hair-loss measures.

Photograph: Julia Forbes

As for my eczema, the iRestore Elite did quell my scalp flare-ups, but I don't think I'd throw down so much money for just that. For hair regrowth, that's a totally different story. My husband was already using Rogaine before the iRestore Elite showed up. But combined with the helmet and iRestore's hair-growth products and supplements, he experienced greater results. For those pursuing thicker hair at home, the iRestore Elite is surprisingly effective.

Julia Forbes is a product writer and reviewer for the WIRED Reviews team, focused on all things related to sleeping well: mattresses, sheets, pillows, toppers, and tech. She is a Spencer Institute-certified Sleep Science coach and has been testing mattresses and sleep products for more than five years. Previously, Julia ... Read More

entries.title: Jensen Huang Apologizes to Nvidia Employees in First All-Hands Since His Return
entries.summary: The Nvidia CEO opened up about his personal life, defended his reinstatement, and acknowledged that his intense management style had hurt his staff.
entries.content:
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told employees on Tuesday that the company’s code of conduct allows room for a “second chance,” that succession planning is a “flawed’ process,” and that he would work to rein in his “insanely intense” management style, according to remarks reviewed by WIRED.

During his first all-hands since returning as CEO, Huang acknowledged that he violated the company’s policies and made some “very serious personal mistakes” that damaged his relationships with his wife and two children and prompted him to resign. But he said Nvidia’s board of directors made the appropriate decision for the company in welcoming him back. He added that the board made that call, not “the highest levels of our government.”

Huang spoke for about an hour, offering deeply personal thoughts about his therapy sessions and drawing applause at times from employees at Nvidia’s Silicon Valley headquarters as he spoke about the company’s success and future. He didn’t take any questions. While some Nvidia employees celebrated Huang’s return, others remained concerned about his behavior and the board’s decision to reinstate him.

“This is going to be the hardest company meeting I’ve ever done, and the second hardest meeting I have ever done,” Huang said as he began to speak. “The hardest meeting I’ve ever done was with my wife.”

Nvidia’s board accepted Huang’s resignation earlier this month, citing concerns about his personal behavior and lack of candor following news reports about extramarital affairs, including one with a woman accused of having ties to Chinese intelligence services. The very same board reinstated him on Monday, just 11 days later, after receiving fresh assurances from Huang and learning from the Trump administration that he was not under federal criminal scrutiny and his return would not be a risk to national security.

Huang and Nvidia, though, continue to face other legal and regulatory challenges. The board is investigating whether he was the target of foreign intelligence. US lawmakers expect him to testify before Congress next week. Lawsuits and other probes are ongoing into Nvidia’s disclosures about Huang’s behavior and its compliance with US export controls on chips.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Got a Tip?
Are you a current or former Nvidia employee who has information to share? We’d like to hear from you. Using a nonwork phone or computer, contact the reporter securely on Signal at Peard33.24

Huang told staffers that he has been going to therapy “every day for an hour and a half” and that it’s “been helping me a lot.” He added that he “made some very serious personal mistakes. I hurt my family, I hurt my wife.”

While Huang said he had never knowingly made a decision contrary to the company’s interests, he conceded that “in this one area” he had lacked “the courage” to disclose information that he knew would hurt his family, seemingly referring to the extramarital affairs.

“The board and I spent the whole weekend together, and they, of course, they've been contemplating, and they've been collecting facts,” Huang said. “They came to the judgment that they would like to invite me back as the CEO, to give me a second chance.”

The CEO emphasized that Nvidia’s code of conduct, much of which he said he wrote himself, still governs how employees are expected to treat one another and is intended to “create an environment that’s safe for people.”

Huang told employees that violations of the code would not be tolerated. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” he said. “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” would factor in.

“It has to always be evaluated in the context of the human,” he said. “And this company has been more than gracious, more than thoughtful, more than fair in giving me a second chance.”

Huang also pushed back against the notion that he had received preferential treatment because of his status in Silicon Valley. “There are rumors on the internet that apparently I’m a tech bro, and therefore I’m back,” Huang said. He rejected the suggestion that he was above the law or Nvidia’s code of conduct.

Later in the meeting, Huang addressed criticism of his self-described “deeply intense, insanely intense” management style, acknowledging that his behavior had at times negatively affected employees. While Huang maintained that the intensity he brings to his job elevates those around him, he conceded that he sometimes takes things too far.

“It disempowers them, and that’s not right,” Huang said. The Nvidia CEO said he needed to figure out how to maintain his level of dedication to the company without hurting the people who work there.

“I need to hold myself to a higher standard at this time,” Huang said. He said that he would undergo a 360-degree performance review, soliciting feedback as often as monthly from people who work with him. The CEO added that he would be the first and only person at Nvidia to undergo such a review and that he did not want to institute the practice companywide.

Huang acknowledged during the meeting that Trump was a vocal supporter of Nvidia but insisted that politics played no role in how the company operated. “It is absolutely true that President Trump really, really loves our company,” Huang said. “He is my president. And I’ll do everything I can to help this president.”

Huang said he would take the same approach with future US presidents. “We are the most apolitical company,” he said. “I don’t love that we talk about politics here. I love that we talk about work here.”

Huang also sought to reassure women at Nvidia, describing himself as “one of our greatest advocates for creating an environment for women” and touting the company’s flexible work policies, which he said allow employees to simultaneously build their families and careers.

“If I did anything that put that in jeopardy, I cannot tell you how sad I am, and I’ll do everything I can to fix it,” Huang said.

After Huang’s resignation, he and the company’s board received criticism from Wall Street for not having an obvious internal successor in line. Huang addressed the issue head-on during the company meeting. “I don't believe in succession planning; I think it’s flawed,” he said, specifying that the concept may make sense but the implementation often causes issues.

Huang described each of his 60 reports as CEOs of their own units who could step up when he eventually leaves. “It creates resilience, and it creates the opportunity, which is ultimately the responsibility of the board, to give them the opportunity to decide at that time what the world needed, what the company needed, and be able to choose from a large collection of amazing people,” he said.

The CEO also argued that his brief absence had demonstrated Nvidia’s ability to operate without him. “I promise you, whether I’m here or not, this company is wired up to execute, execute, and execute,” Huang said.

entries.title: The 24 Very Best Amazon Black Friday Deals to Get Now (2026)
entries.summary: For die-hard Amazon shoppers, the retailer’s “Black Friday Week” sale is now live. Grab these deals on our favorite (and tested) products through November 30.
entries.content:
Amazon’s Black Friday deals are a go. Its “Black Friday Week” sale runs from now until November 30 (Cyber Monday), giving shoppers a head start on holiday shopping. To help you sift through the many products, we’ve highlighted some of our favorites below. If you’re a big Amazon shopper, now is a great time to fill those holiday wish lists and spend Black Friday with friends and family.

Check out our guide to the best Early Black Friday deals, plus standing desk deals, Home Depot appliance savings, and early tech deals.

Updated November 24: We’ve updated this story with more deals on products we’ve tested and recommend.

Jump To

Best Amazon Black Friday Tech Deals

When Apple raised prices earlier this year, the once-affordable MacBook Air now starts at $1,300. The MacBook Air is still the best Apple laptop for most people, even some pro users, thanks to the M5 chipset’s power and efficiency. This Black Friday deal brings the 13-inch base model to $ 104, close to its pre-increase price. Its 15-inch sibling is also on sale for $1,199, down from $1,499. (Note: The 13-inch MacBook Air was discounted as low as $989—an excellent deal—earlier this week, but has increased slightly. Pricing may fluctuate through Black Friday and into Cyber Monday.)

The Arc Ultra is a soundbar that does it right, delivering great all-around performance from a single speaker. Our current pick as the best soundbar you can buy, the Arc Ultra supports Dolby Atmos and DTS:X surround sound to create cinema-quality audio in your living room. For a true surround setup, the Sonos Ultimate Immersive Set with Arc Ultra is also on sale and includes a subwoofer and two additional speakers.

The best iPad for most people isn’t one of Apple’s more powerful options, which says a lot. The base iPad runs on the older A16 chipset, but it can handle most of what people use a tablet for: streaming entertainment, web browsing, email, drawing, and even light productivity work. It’s great for casual users, including kids. This Black Friday deal brings the price closer to its previous MSRP, before Apple’s price increase. Check out more Black Friday iPad Deals.

While you can often find this router at this sale price, it’s still a deal for the best budget Wi-Fi router for a small home. It’s not the most powerful router, and it doesn’t support the 6 GHz band, but if your needs are basic, it will more than suffice.

With a WIRED rating of 9 out of 10, the XM6 is one of our favorite over-ear headphones, combining comfort with great sound quality and noise cancellation. This is the lowest price on Amazon; however, it has dropped to this price before. Note that Walmart and Best Buy are also offering the XM6 at this sale price.

Good gaming laptops are never cheap, and they’ve become even more expensive this year. If you need a recommendation that balances performance and budget, we recommend the Asus ROG Strix G16 with an Nvidia GeForce RTX 5060, one of our favorite budget gaming laptops. We prefer the RTX 5070 option, but it’s nearly $3,000. This on-sale model is more attainable.

The latest Echo Show 11 is our recommendation for the Best Alexa Smart Display. WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell found the screen bright and crisp, with immersive sound quality. Since the sale price matches the regular price of the smaller Echo Show 8, it’s a good deal—just $5 more than the sale price during Amazon’s October Prime Day event.

The Pixel 11-series phones from Google are among our favorite Android devices. Loaded with the latest software and Gemini AI features, the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro, and Pixel 11 Pro XL are our pick as the smartest Android smartphones. They’re also the only non-iPhones to support Qi2 wireless charging and magnetic mounting, so you can use MagSafe accessories. During Black Friday, you can get all for under $1,000 each—a terrific deal for a flagship phone—and they’re at their lowest price ever on Amazon.

High-quality three-in-one charging stands look terrific on a bedside table, but many cost over $100. This one from Mophie is one of our favorites, and it’s 49 percent off on Amazon right now.

The AirTag seems to be on sale all the time, but no matter—it’s currently the lowest price on Amazon and cheaper than buying from Apple. It’s one of the best Bluetooth trackers. If you can swing it, go for the four-pack.

Alongside the AirTag, the AirPods Max 2 and AirPods Pro 3 are also on sale. These are well-regarded among WIRED testers, but we recommend waiting until after Thanksgiving to see if they drop further—don’t worry, they are often on sale.

Phone accessories are aplenty on Amazon, but few look as good as Moft’s. You can pick up this ingenious wallet-kickstand hybrid that attaches to an iPhone via MagSafe, or peruse the rest of Moft’s Black Friday deals.

You can expect Amazon’s own devices to go on sale during Black Friday. While Blink’s security cameras didn’t make our short list, WIRED reviewer Simon Hill still thinks they’re worth considering, especially if you’re on a budget. A downer is that they only work with Alexa, but if that’s your smart home setup, it’s NBD. The latest version of its pan-tilt camera is usually $50, but it’s 60 percent off right now.

WIRED’s audio editor won’t stop praising Soundcore products, but he’s not wrong: This nascent brand (soon to be rebranded as Anker, its parent company) makes terrific audio products without the premium price. WIRED reviewer Louryn Strampe included this Bluetooth boom box in a roundup of her favorite festival gear. It’s the lowest price ever on Amazon currently, but it’s not the cheapest—keep an eye out at other retailers during Black Friday.

This EcoFlow portable battery is WIRED reviewer Simon Hill’s pick as the best power bank for laptops. It has a large 27,650-mAh capacity, which is plenty for charging smaller devices too. It’s great for travel since it’s allowed on a plane, and it has a retractable USB-C cable, so you can leave extras at home.

At $359, the second-gen Bose QuietComfort over-ear headphones seem overpriced considering the competition. But when they’re on sale at $199 to $219 (depending on the color), they suddenly become a great buy. As expected from Bose, the noise cancellation and sound quality are excellent. They are also comfortable, making them great travel companions. Note that the first-gen version is also on sale for $169 (it’s frequently at this price), but it’s outdated, and we think you should spend $30 to $50 more on the latest version instead.

Amazon Early Black Friday Home and Kitchen Deals

Gone are the days of putting up holiday lights and then taking them down, only to do it again the next year. These outdoor lights are designed to stay up permanently; when they’re not displaying colorful holiday lights, they can shine white for regular everyday lighting. They work with any smart home platform, so you can control them via an app or a voice assistant.

WIRED Reviews Editor Kat Merck is our resident bird expert, having tested numerous bird feeders and doing extensive research on her feathered friends who visit her home. One of the best bird feeders she’s used is on sale at Amazon at the lowest price ever. The Kiwibit Bird Feeder 2 is easy to clean and has a solar roof for wire-free camera charging. The app even has a handy bird-identification feature to help you determine what species stopped by.

It seems like every appliance maker offers an air fryer, but if you want the best, the Typhur Dome 2 should be at the top of your shortlist. It’s also on sale this Black Friday, which makes this “splurge” item a bit easier on the holiday budget. Our reviewer found it works fast during testing, and it can bake as well as cook a pizza or steak.

As a premium home appliance maker, Dyson doesn’t make cheap products. Which is why Black Friday is a good time to see what might go on sale. Right now, our top pick for the most affordable Dyson vacuum cleaner is even cheaper—the lowest price we’ve seen yet. It works on both hard and carpeted floors, and its brush system can handle all sorts of debris.

Love them or hate them, but pod-based coffee makers are popular for their convenience. The Nespresso Vertuo Pop+ is our recommended espresso pod maker, and the Deluxe model is under $100. It has a larger water tank than the standard version, and the Vertuo pods are recyclable. For more savings on coffee-related products, check out our Early Black Friday Espresso Machine Deals.

WIRED’s home-cleaning expert, Nena Farrell, recommended only three robot vacuums, naming this Eufy floor-sweeping automaton her budget pick. It’s 53 percent off right now—the lowest price ever on Amazon—for a robovac with great suction power and a self-cleaning roller mop.

With quality espresso machines costing $500 and more (way, way more), a budget option seems improbable. Yet, this De’Longhi fits the bill. One of our recommended models, it usually costs around $200 or just a little more, but you can snag one for $150 if you’ve been wanting to get into the third-wave coffee game. It’s a great price, but we’ve seen it go as low as $120 in past sales.
